note: Compares pre-, in- and post-processing mitigations and when each fits, which supports practical audit recommendations.
title: A Review on Fairness in Machine Learning

reading.body:
Fairness in machine learning is a mature research field with a settled structure: methods act before, during, or after training, and the choice depends on the situation.

The review's organizing principle is timing. Pre-processing changes the data, in-processing changes the training objective, and post-processing changes the outputs. That framing matters because it turns fairness from a vague aspiration into a decision about where in a pipeline to intervene, and each stage carries different costs and constraints.

For AI systems specifically, the review is scoped mainly to classification. It covers how bias arises, how fairness is defined and measured, and which mitigation fits which scenario, with some attention to fairness questions outside classification. It is a map of techniques, not a benchmark of which technique wins.

What the data does not cover is scale. There is no discussion here of compute, data centers, or power, and nothing about how the cost of fairness interventions changes as models grow. The 734 citations indicate the review is widely relied on, but citation counts measure influence, not whether the recommended methods hold up in production systems.

explain_beginner: Machine learning now helps make many important decisions, such as who gets a loan, a job, or a place at college. This review explains that these systems can be unfair even when nobody intends harm. It gathers common ways to define fairness, ways to measure it, and methods to improve it. Those methods are grouped by when they act, before training, during training, or after training. The authors compare them to see which approach suits different situations. This matters because people need to know how to check and improve automated decisions that affect their lives.
explain_business: Organizations increasingly use machine learning for decisions in hiring, lending, education, healthcare, and other areas. This review shows that unfair outcomes can occur even without deliberate bias. It explains how to identify and measure fairness and compares methods for improving it before, during, or after model development. The authors assess which methods fit different situations. For executives, this means fairness should be treated as a managed part of AI projects, not an afterthought. The paper can inform decisions about when to audit models, which mitigation stage to choose, and how to set practical fairness checks before deploying automated systems.
explain_practitioner: This paper is a review of fairness in machine learning, focused mainly on classification. It covers why bias and unfairness arise in algorithms, along with how fairness is commonly defined and measured. The authors organize methods that improve fairness into three stages, before model training, during model training, and after model training. They then compare these approaches to clarify which ones fit different scenarios. The review also looks at newer research areas in fairness outside classification. For engineers and researchers, the value is a structured map of available techniques and when each may be suitable, which can guide method selection and fairness audits in practical machine learning work.
